blocks.prompt: The Moon Is Always Round
blocks.text: The moon does not make its own light. There is no lamp inside it. The light you see is sunlight bouncing off gray rock. The sun shines on one half of the moon all the time. The other half stays dark. But the moon moves around the Earth. So each night we see a little more of the bright half, or a little less. That is why the moon looks like a big circle one week and a thin curve the next. It takes about 29 days to go from one full moon to the next full moon. The moon never changes shape. It is always round. We just cannot always see the whole round part.

3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: Why the Moon Changes Shape
blocks.text: The moon looks different every night, but it never actually changes shape. It is a ball of rock, and it stays a ball of rock. Here is what is really going on. The moon makes no light of its own. Every bit of moonlight you have ever seen is sunlight bouncing off gray rock and dust. The sun always lights up exactly half of the moon, the half that faces it. The other half stays dark. That never stops being true. The moon takes about a month to travel all the way around the Earth. As it travels, we look at it from a different angle each night. Sometimes we see the whole lit half at once, and we call that a full moon. Sometimes the lit half is turned away from us and we see almost nothing, which we call a new moon. In between, we catch the lit half at a slant: a thin crescent, then a half circle, then a fat lopsided shape called a gibbous moon. So the moon is not growing and shrinking. You are just walking around a lit ball and seeing it from new places. Long before there were calendars on the wall, people counted time by those shapes. That is why the word month sounds so much like the word moon.

4.title: The Moon Is Always Round
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Phases come from angle, not shadow

blocks.prompt: The Half That Faces the Sun
blocks.text: Ask most people what makes the moon change shape and they will tell you the Earth's shadow creeps across it. That answer is wrong, and it is wrong in an interesting way. Start with two facts. First, the moon has no light of its own. It is dark gray rock, about as reflective as an old parking lot, and it glows only because sunlight lands on it. Second, sunlight arrives from one direction, so it can light only one half of the moon at a time. The half facing the sun is bright. The half facing away is black. That is true every second of every day, and it never changes. What changes is you. The moon circles the Earth once a month or so, which swings your view of it around. When the moon sits roughly between the Earth and the sun, its lit half points away from you and you see almost nothing. Astronomers call that a new moon. When the Earth sits between the sun and the moon, the lit half faces you completely and you get a full moon, which is why a full moon rises at about the time the sun sets. Every night in between, you catch the lit half at an angle: a sliver, then a half circle, then a fat lopsided shape called gibbous, from a Latin word meaning humped. So where does the Earth's shadow come in? It is real, and it does fall on the moon, but only rarely and only for a few hours. That is a lunar eclipse, and it happens two or three times a year at most. Phases happen every single night. They have nothing to do with shadow. They are about which part of a lit ball you happen to be standing where you can see.

5.title: The Moon Is Always Round
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Eight Names for One Rock
blocks.text: The moon is the easiest object in the sky to find and one of the easiest to misunderstand. Almost everyone has been told at some point that its phases come from the Earth's shadow. They do not. The phases are a trick of geometry, and once you see the trick you cannot unsee it. Three facts do all the work. The moon produces no light. It reflects sunlight off rock so dark that a piece of it in your hand would look like charcoal. Sunlight arrives from one direction, so exactly half the moon is lit at any instant, no more and no less. And the moon orbits the Earth, finishing a lap in about 27.3 days but returning to the same phase only every 29.5 days. That gap exists because the Earth refuses to hold still. It carries us around the sun while the moon circles us, so the moon must travel a little farther each cycle to line up the same way again. Put the three facts together. Your view of the lit half swings around as the moon travels. When the moon lies roughly between the Earth and the sun, its bright side faces away and it vanishes into daytime glare. That is the new moon. A few nights later a thin crescent hangs low in the west after sunset, and it grows, or waxes, night after night. At first quarter you see half a disc, even though the moon has finished only a quarter of its orbit. The name tracks the orbit, not the picture. It keeps swelling into a gibbous shape, from the Latin gibbus, meaning hump, until the Earth sits between the sun and the moon and the whole lit face turns our way. That is the full moon, and it rises almost exactly as the sun sets. Then the shape shrinks, or wanes, back through gibbous, last quarter, and crescent, and disappears again. The Earth's shadow does touch the moon, but only during a lunar eclipse, and only a few times a year. Phases run every night without fail. The difference matters, because it is the difference between an accident and a clock. Human beings ran their calendars on that clock for thousands of years, and some still do. The word month is the word moon, worn down by use.

6.title: The Moon Is Always Round
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Sidereal orbit 27.3 days, synodic cycle 29.5 days
Terminator: the line between lit and dark
Anaxagoras explained phases around 450 BC
Earthshine: sunlight bounced off Earth onto the moon
Albedo about 0.12, roughly worn asphalt
Tidally locked: one face always toward Earth

blocks.prompt: The Moon Is Always Full
blocks.text: Here is a sentence worth sitting with: the moon is always full. It is always a sphere, and the sun always lights exactly half of that sphere. Nothing about the moon changes between Tuesday and Thursday. What changes is the angle you are standing at. That is the whole of it, and yet the phases of the moon may be the most widely misunderstood thing in the sky. Ask a room of adults and a good number will tell you the Earth's shadow creeps across the moon and carves out the crescent. It is a reasonable guess, and it is wrong. The Earth's shadow does fall on the moon, but only during a lunar eclipse, only when the three bodies line up precisely, and only a couple of times a year. Phases run every night without fail. A cause that appears twice a year cannot explain an effect that appears 365 nights a year. The real explanation was worked out roughly 2,500 years ago. Anaxagoras, a Greek thinker living in Athens, argued that the moon is not a god or a lamp but a rock, that it borrows its light from the sun, and that both the changing shape and the occasional eclipse follow from where that rock happens to sit. He was reportedly prosecuted for saying so. He was also right. Follow the geometry. Sunlight arrives in essentially parallel rays from one direction, so half the moon is lit and half is dark, permanently. The line dividing them is called the terminator. The moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit the Earth but 29.5 days to return to the same phase, because the Earth does not hold still. It carries us around the sun the whole time, so the moon must swing a little farther each cycle to line up again. As the moon moves, your line of sight cuts across the lit half at a new angle every night. Near new moon you are looking almost straight at the dark side. Near full moon you are looking almost straight at the lit side. Everything else is in between: crescent, quarter, gibbous, a smooth sweep from nothing to everything and back. Two details reward attention. The first is that a quarter moon looks like a half. It is called first quarter because the moon has finished one quarter of its orbit, not because a quarter of the disc is lit. The name tracks the clock, not the picture. The second is earthshine. On a thin crescent, look at the dark portion and you can often make out a faint gray circle, the rest of the moon, dimly there. That light is sunlight that struck the Earth, bounced off our oceans and clouds, crossed a quarter of a million miles, and landed on lunar rock. Leonardo da Vinci reasoned that out in a notebook around 1510. Skywatchers had a phrase for the sight long before anyone knew the cause: the old moon in the new moon's arms. The moon is also far darker than it looks. Its surface returns only about twelve percent of the light that hits it, roughly the reflectiveness of worn asphalt. It looks brilliant to you only because it hangs against a black sky. None of this is trivia. Almost every ancient calendar was a moon calendar, because the moon is a clock anyone can read for free, without instruments and without permission. The Islamic year still runs on it. The date of Easter still depends on it. The English word month is the word moon, worn smooth by several thousand years of mouths. The shape overhead tonight is not information about the moon. It is information about where you are standing.
